definition: Congeal means to thicken or solidify, especially when a liquid cools into a solid mass.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word congeal. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know congeal should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The gravy forgotten on the counter began to congeal into a pale, rubbery layer.
To thicken is only to grow denser while still flowing, whereas to congeal is to set into a mass that no longer pours at all.
Congealing leaves behind a soft, spoonable solid, but hardening goes further, leaving something firm and unyielding.

Solidify means to become fully firm or solid, and it also covers deliberate processes and figurative ones - concrete solidifies, plans solidify, support solidifies. Congeal is narrower and more physical: a cooling liquid sets into a soft, often unappetizing mass. Concrete solidifies into something you can stand on; leftover gravy merely congeals.

Coagulate describes a liquid clotting into clumps and curds through a chemical change - blood coagulates at a wound, milk coagulates when acid hits it. Congeal is about temperature: a liquid cools and sets smoothly into one soft mass. Blood coagulates whether warm or cold; gravy congeals simply because it cools.

Congeal means to thicken or solidify, especially when a liquid cools into a solid mass.
A cook poured the hot drippings from a roasting pan into a metal bowl and set it near an open window.
Within an hour the liquid had turned cloudy at the edges, then stiffened toward the center.
By morning it had thickened into a solid pale cake that a spoon could stand upright in.
Nothing had been added to it; the fat only needed to cool in order to congeal.
A liquid cooled and set into a solid mass with nothing added to it, which is exactly what congeal describes.
neutral register; common in cooking, biology, and figurative writing
In ordinary use congeal is intransitive: a liquid congeals on its own as it cools, rather than someone congealing it.
Writers also use it figuratively for scattered ideas, rumors, or crowds that settle into one fixed mass, as in 'the separate accounts congealed into a single story.'
